subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have two petitions. The first deals with Bill C-55 which threatens Canada's traditional commitment to assisting refugees and sets out measures designed to keep most refugee claimants out of the country as opposed to ensuring that genuine claimants are given protection.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings for claimants before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings for every applicant in Canada, and the right to appeal on the basis of fact.

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-OPPOSITION TO CORPORATE PLAN
speechtext:
The second petition deals with the Post Office.
Whereas the federal Government's proposal to seek financial self-sufficiency by 1988 for Canada Post Corporation will result in cut-backs, deterioration in service and consequently will be at the expense of service to Canadian consumers, the petitioners call upon Parliament to instruct the Government to make improved service the highest priority of Canada Post and abandon the policy of closing rural Post Offices and cancelling rural routes.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to present a petition from a number of residents of the Cities of Toronto, Montreal and other municipalities in Ontario and Quebec. They object to Bill C-55. They point out that the concept of a safe third country has no foundation in law and no definition and therefore subjects the refugee process to undue political and diplomatic pressures. They also point out that a better alternative has been provided by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration which has the support of churches, the labour movement, the Bar Association and many other groups.
Therefore they request Parliament to withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of claims of refugee claimants before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings for every applicant in Canada, and the right to appeal on the basis of fact. In duty-bound, your petitioners will ever pray.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since giving this Bill second reading about 10 days ago the House has passed Bill C-71 which deals with war criminals and those who have committed crimes against humanity. The five motions which we have presented at this time are all consequential amendments to the passage of Bill C-71 which was passed last week. Pursuant to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I will deal with these five motions in one address.
The purpose of the motion to amend Clause 2 of Bill C-84 is to add "war criminals'" to the list of types of persons who may be made the subject of security reports leading to deportation from Canada.
Bill C-71 would add a new inadmissible class of persons to the list of inadmissible classes in Subsection 19(1) of the Immigration Act, 1976. This new inadmissible class, which would be described in Section 19(1 )(j) of the Immigration Act, precludes the admission to Canada of persons who there are reasonable grounds to believe had committed a war crime or crime against humanity.
The effect of Clause 2 of Bill C-84 is to continue the existing process for handling security matters concerning permanent residents of Canada. This process, set out in Sections 39 and 40 of the Immigration Act, involves a security report signed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Solicitor General, a review by the Security Intelligence Review Committee, and a recommendation to the Governor in Council.
It should be noted with reference to Bill C-71 that the provisions regarding the inadmissibility of permanent residents who may have committed a war crime is not retroactive. These provisions will prevent the admission to Canada for permanent residence of any person, after the proclamation of Bill C-71, who has committed a war crime or crime against humanity and will allow for the deportation of permanent residents who commit such odious crimes after the coming into force of Section 19(1 )(j).
I am sure that all Members will agree that persons who have committed a war crime or crime against humanity ought to be treated in the same manner as other persons who pose a security risk to Canada. This motion to amend will ensure that that is the case.
The purpose of the motion to amend Clause 3 of Bill C-84 is to add a reference to "war criminals" to Section 40 of the Immigration Act. As mentioned earlier in reference to Clause 2 of Bill C-84, Sections 39 and 40 of the Immigration Act set out the process for handling security matters involving

August 31, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
permanent residents of Canada. This motion is therefore consequential on the addition of the reference to Section 19(l)(j), which describes war criminals, to Clause 2 of Bill C-84. Clause 2 amends Section 39 of the Act.
The purpose of the motion to amend Clause 4 of Bill C-84 is to add a reference to "war criminals" to the list of types of persons who may be made the subject of security certificates leading to deportation from Canada. As mentioned in reference to Clause 2 of Bill C-84, Bill C-71 would add a new Section 19(l)(j) to the Immigration Act thereby making war criminals inadmissible to Canada.
Clause 4 of Bill C-84 establishes a new process for handling security matters involving persons who are not permanent residents of Canada, that is, for example, visitors, refugee claimants, and illegal aliens in Canada. The new process involves a security report signed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Solicitor General and a review by the Federal Court.
I am sure that all Members will want to support this motion to amend Clause 4 to ensure that once Bill C-71 is proclaimed war criminals will be treated under the Immigration Act in the same manner as other security risks.
The purpose of the amendment to Clause 5 of Bill C-84 is to ensure that when Bill C-71 is proclaimed war criminals will be denied access to Canada's refugee determination system.
The United Nations Convention relating to the status of refugees provides in Article IF that:
The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that he has committed a crime against peace, a war crime, or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crimes.
The UN Convention lists war criminals as persons considered not to be deserving of international protection. As a result, we wish to deny access to the refugee determination system to minimize the prospect that such persons will be able to manipulate the system in order to delay their removal from Canada.
Finally, there is the amendment to Clause 12. The purpose of this amendment to Clause 12 would be to add a reference to war crimes to the new provisions established in Bill C-84 for detention at the port of entry for investigation of identity or security risk.
Clause 12 of Bill C-84 would establish a new Section 104.1 of the Immigration Act. This Section would permit the Minister to issue a certificate requiring detention of a person upon arrival in Canada for up to 28 days for investigation of whether that person may pose a security risk to Canadians.
The present motion to amend Clause 12 by adding a reference to paragraph 19(l)(j) of the Immigration Act as would be established by Bill C-71, would ensure that persons
suspected of being war criminals would be treated in the same manner as other persons who are suspected of posing a security risk.
Finally, I wish to emphasize that nothing in these amendments will interfere with our ability to prosecute war criminals in Canada. Removal provisions do not overrule or override the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see the Parliamentary Secretary steering this Bill so competently through the House. While I am very happy to hear his voice, and follow the logic of his approach, I must say that with two Ministers of Immigration in the House, whose combined skills are perhaps not as good as the Parliamentary Secretary alone, 1 cannot understand why they should not be here today to deal with their Bill and guide us through the report stage.
Where is your critic?

When one considers that for some reason, which is hard to understand, the Tories decided to have two Ministers in charge of immigration, at least one of them ought to be here, particularly in view of the shabby way in which they have handled questions in Question Period when we were grilling the Government on a number of questions related to Bill C-84.
I must confirm my confidence in the Parliamentary Secretary and say that actually, in a way, 1 am reassured by the fact that his presence here today shows that his skill and competence is being recognized by the Government.
The amendments to Clauses 1, 4, 7, 11, and 18, which were put forward by the Parliamentary Secretary, are important because they deal with the processing of war criminals. We on this side of the House concur in the necessity of introducing these clauses and debating them under one motion as you us to do a few moments ago.
Therefore, on behalf of the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), who is due to arrive any moment, I will be very glad to concur. I believe he has been held up on constituency business, which I believe everyone understands.
He is not the proponent of the Bill and there is a big difference. The proponent of the Bill is the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and that is why I am saying he should be here.
In any case, we concur with the motion before us.

Mr. Speaker, we support this group of motions relating to this amendment. We are also very pleased that the war criminals Bill has been passed. Of course, these motions are consequent upon it.
We support these motions, notwithstanding that we oppose
those parts of Bill C-84 to which these motions relate.
Specifically, we oppose the denial of access to the refugee
August 31, 1987

process for the several classes of people who are referred to in this motion. We disagree with the interpretation that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has given, based on a quotation from one aspect of the United Nations Convention for Refugees.
Representatives from the United Nations High Commission for Refugees made it very plain when they spoke to us during our committee hearings on this Bill that, while they do not grant the absolute demand for protection to war criminals and the others described in this motion, they still ask that the decision to find the person as one of those so described should be made as part of determining the refugee status which the person has claimed. We are talking about people who have claimed refugee status but are found to be inadmissible on these grounds.
The United Nations Convention does not require that Canada or any country admit somebody that it finds inadmissible on these grounds. It does not even require that Canada observe the rule against returning that person directly or indirectly to the country where he fears persecution. Therefore, the right of Canada to do what it thinks is necessary for its security, and necessary in accordance with the war criminals Bill, is not in any way infringed or challenged either by the United Nations Convention regarding the protection of the status of refugees or by the decisions of the executive of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees. This was made quite clear to us by their representative who spoke to our committee a couple of weeks ago.
However, they do urge that their procedure be followed. Their procedure includes not only recognition or non-recognition of a person's claim to refugee status, but also recognition of the facts of the crimes of this sort for which the person may either be convicted or very reasonably suspected of committing.
In their view, the difference it makes is that if there is a person in Canada who is convicted or suspected of those crimes and therefore considered unacceptable, inadmissible in Canada-of course leaving aside the extradition at the request of another country which is based on other legislation- nevertheless, in regard to refugee status, Canada ought to allow the refugee process to continue its full course, including consideration of that security risk or crime, war crime, or crime against humanity.
Considering both facts, both the crime and the fact of refugee status, it might make a difference in how that person's situation would be handled. It might be possible, if the United Nations High Commission so wished, to have that person sent to some other country than the one from which he fled. There are war crimes and there are war crimes, and this has come out during the debate on the war crimes Bill.
Not everyone is completely at one about the exact definition or scope of the definition of war crimes. Therefore, the United Nations prefers that we follow the rule it has adopted, which is
Immigration Act, 1976
not binding on us but is recommended. It prefers that we do not deny access to the refugee states process even to these people. In fact, there have been very few cases, perhaps a couple of dozen, who have come anywhere close to this category in the last couple of decades in Canada.
It is not a burdensome item and the UNHCR prefers that we keep the principle clear of not denying refugee status to a person who has claimed it. But it is an agreement with us that after that status has been granted, and in the case of someone who is also found to fall into this inadmissible category, Canada then is free to deport that person according to our own laws but it wishes we would consult with the UNHCR before we do that.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we would be supporting this clause, although we will be opposing certain parts of the Bill with which this clause deals.

Motion No. 2
That Bill C-84 be amended by deleting Clause 2.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Clause 2 and Clause 3 are really, as explained in the notes, consequential on Clause 4. However, I understand we have to take them up as they come.
The effect of Clause 2 or Clause 3 is to separate out certain groups from an action that is taken by Clause 4. The effect of the three clauses together is to set up a new procedure around the matter of security certificates. In the existing legislation we have provision for security certificates.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) together may sign a security certificate which accuses a certain person of being in effect a threat to the security of Canada. They are not required by law to provide information as to the nature of the action the person is accused of committing, nor are they required to provide any of the evidence. The argument for that contrary to our otherwise normal legal procedure in Canada is that to describe the act or the evidence might of itself endanger the security of Canada or the security of certain persons. This provision has been in force for some years and I am told that in the last couple of decades about 23 people have been accused under that provision.
There is a limited degree of protection of the rights of the persons so accused. The charge and the evidence are reviewed by the Security Intelligence Review Committee, the same body that was set up by Parliament to monitor the work of CSIS, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. The Security Intelligence Review Committee will review the information, the accusation and the evidence, and it will describe some of it to the accused person, to the extent it believes it can give that
information without endangering the security of Canada or the safety of any persons. The accused person is allowed to respond to that limited part of the information. The Security Intelligence Review Committee then makes a recommendation to the Minister as to whether the certificate should be sustained or not. If the certificate is sustained, and if the Minister judges that the person is a threat to the security of Canada, that person may be deported.
What is being done by the new law is to say that while the earlier law applies to Canadian citizens, if they are so charged, and to permanent residents of Canada, if they are so charged, it does not apply to others such as visitors on a visitor's visa or to people who have come in without any adequate documentation such as many refugee claimants claiming what we have provided in our law as the Inland Refugee Claim procedure. Those people, including those refugee claimants, instead of having the certificate reviewed by the SIRC will have it reviewed by the Supreme Court. We will be opposing that when it is dealt with under the amendments relating to Clause 4.
I will not go at length into the reasons for opposing it now. Since we are opposing the creation of this new procedure for those who are neither citizens nor permanent residents of Canada, we therefore oppose the separation of those people from citizens and permanent residents in the division of this law into two parts. There seems to us to be no sufficient reasons shown why the matter should be put before the Federal Court of Appeal rather than the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
Very briefly, the explanation given by certain persons, staff and certain Members of Parliament, is that it will expedite the action. That seems very questionable since there seems to be great evidence that the Federal Court has as great a backlog, if not a greater backlog of business, than does the SIRC. Although at present the SIRC meets only monthly it is able to meet in panels or as single persons in order to deal with matters as they come up.
To my understanding there has been no delay, or no undue delay, in having these cases, the few that have occurred, looked at by the SIRC. There may well be a delay of months, according to the backlog of the Federal Court. That would be potentially injurious to the accused person who, of course, is being detained. That sort of delay and prolongation of the process certainly increases the administrative burden of the Department and of the justice system.
Further, the Federal Court has no expertise as such in security matters. Whether some individual members may have a background in security or not, the court as such has no expertise in that area. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister pointed out during debate at second reading, the court has access to the security information provided by CSIS. It has the same access as does the review committee. That is
August 31, 1987

not the question. The question is about the court's familiarity and expertise in evaluating such information.
The whole point of the review is that the matter should not be left merely to the fact that the security authorities have presented certain evidence. That evidence has to be weighed. We have a body which is appointed for two special purposes, and one is to weigh that evidence. Over several years it has developed a recognized competence in doing that.
The Federal Court is a court which judges legal procedures. It reviews how a case has been handled to see whether or not it has been handled according to law. It is not within its expertise to handle matters of fact. It is certainly not within its expertise to weigh matters of security. Therefore we believe that as a matter of justice the group should not be divided to separate non-permanent residents from the rest.
We also believe there may very well be the occasion of a Charter challenge under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In the general spirit of the Singh decision of two and a half years ago, it may be that the Supreme Court will find that it is unconstitutional, contrary to the Charter, to deny as good a hearing to non-permanent residents as is available to permanent residents. That was certainly the spirit of the Singh decision. It would be consistent with that decision if the Supreme Court found that in this case.
Rather than waiting perhaps two or three years for a Supreme Court challenge, with the exception of that and with the trouble that may accrue to individuals in the meantime, I hope that the Government will agree to the amendment that I will put later which would withdraw that amendment to Clause 4. I am therefore asking that we withdraw this consequential amendment now.

Mr. Speaker, unlike the government Members in committee, we listened to those who appeared before our committee on Bill C-84. We carefully developed a position whereby we concluded that Clause 2, which gives considerable powers to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, should be removed. The reason is this. The Minister would be given the power to arbitrarily sign a certificate against a person without the benefit of the report by the committee. I am referring to the Security Intelligence Review Committee. This is an arbitrary power that was objected to by a number of organizations which appeared before the committee.
For instance, the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees commented, saying that the Security Intelligence Review Committee is doing a good job and has developed expertise in evaluating security certificates. It asked, why that role should be suspended? Actually, it urged that the review task be left with the committee. It felt that the jurisdiction should remain with the Security Intelligence Review Committee. It also argued that the Federal Court does not have the expertise necessary to deal with these matters.
Immigration Act, 1976
We had submissions from the Canadian Bar Association which said it could not see any reason for the inclusion of Clause 2 in the proposed Bill. Representatives of the Bar Association felt that the Federal Court is not an expert tribunal on security issues. They also confirmed that the Security Intelligence Review Committee is doing a good job. They argued that the Federal Court is not fast in making a decision, that a waiting period of six months in the Court of Appeal and longer could take place.
The Canadian Bar Association also felt that the Federal Court would not be any faster than the present process. It reinforced the notion that the committee is adequate. It, too, wanted to leave the jurisdiction with the committee and argued that, perhaps, the decision-making process of the Security Intelligence Review Committee ought to be spread out and expedited.
Amnesty International commented that it cannot see any reason to change the existing system. That association said that often foreign governments do not state the truth about the activities of people they consider as threats-among those foreign governments there are some that are friendly to Canada, as in the case of South Korea-and student security checks.
The Canadian Ethnocultural Council saw no reason to transfer this responsibility to the Federal Court, which already has a heavy case-load, and that council also argued in favour of maintaining the present system.
The Canadian Jewish Congress also supported the existing procedure of the committee. It felt that the procedure for the examination of the validity of the security certificate could be stacked against the claimant; there is no appeal and no crossexamination, the Minister's case would be presented in camera, and the claimant would only receive a summary of the evidence.
The Civil Liberties Association also commented against the change, and the inclusion of Clause 2 to which we object. That organization felt that the Security Intelligence Review Committee is developing a reputation for independence, and that it does have an expertise which ought to be utilized. It also suggested that the committee procedure by the Security Intelligence Review Committee should be maintained.
We also received a submission from the coalition interested in Bill C-84. It argued that the Security Intelligence Review Committee was established to provide for proper review of security decisions. It argued and recommended in favour of leaving the present system in place. It agreed with the Canadian Bar Association proposal to impose time limits. The coalition also stated that there has been no indication that the committee is not working well. It argued that it has now developed considerable experience and knowledge.

There were also submissions from individuals, for example, Mr. Joe Stern, who argued that the role of the committee ought to be continued. The Etobicoke Committee for Fairness to Refugees also felt very strongly that this clause should be removed.
The Inter-Church Committee for Refugees came before the committee. It felt that if there are security worries, the people should go to the refugee division quickly and then a decision could be made regarding security.
It is interesting to note that the United Nations High Commission for Refugees made the observations that we should first determine whether or not a person is a refugee, that a person should be given time to find another country, and that the commission can assist. We would not be helpful if we did not know whether this person was a refugee. The commission argued that we should determine the refugee status first, and then decide on security issues, as it is done presently. This body has been in existence for many years, and it has been engaged in the matter of developing policy and handling the movement of refugees around the globe, and it came forward in favour of removing Clause 2 from this Bill.
Amnesty International also commented on this important matter. It said that the law should give all refugee status claimants the opportunity to be heard on the merits. It developed a rationale for handling cases where the claimants are found to be refugees and security threats.
The submission made by Rabbi Gunther Plaut is also worth considering. He also recommended that we continue with the present system for the reason that criminality is defined differently in different countries. He said that situations may look different when assessed through Canadian eyes. He said it is important to determine that a person is a refugee at the same time as the security assessment is made, and then it is important to decide what to do.
The Canadian Jewish Congress and the coalition, and other people, also appeared before the committee and made comments on this particular clause. I wish to stress that it is important that the Minister pay attention to the arguments advanced by a number of interested parties.
Because the Federal Court is inexperienced in this matter, and the Minister without the benefit of a report by the Security Intelligence Review Committee would have the powers to sign a certificate against a person and file it with the Federal Court, we are voting for the deletion of Clause 2. The present system has proven so far to function properly, and it does not give special powers to a political individual without the benefit of a report from the Security Intelligence Review Committee on which to base a decision.

speechtext:
I appreciate the comments of the two members opposite. As the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) correctly pointed out, the purpose of Clause 2 is to make a distinction between permanent residents and visitors.
Clause 4 will bear that out when there is a distinction made in the manner the two classes of people are treated when a decision has been made.
Broadly speaking, the people that we are talking about in this clause, and again in Section 19(1) of the Immigration Act, are the inadmissible class. Here 1 disagree with the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and I would remind Members opposite that the first purpose of the entire determination system is not to determine whether these people are refugees, but to determine whether they need protection. This was again stated last week in committee. The purpose of the determination system is to decide if these people need protection. In fact, all Members know that some people have found protection elsewhere and have chosen to leave there. As one witness stated, they are shopping for the best place to go.
The second purpose is to provide protection for Canada. We are dealing with an inadmissible class, people who have been convicted of crime, who may be security risks, and now, on the amended version, who may have been guilty of war crimes. Surely Members opposite would concede that there is a rationale for treating visitors differently from permanent residents. Permanent residents do have rights, as do citizens. They can work. They have a right to employment and to the social services of Canada. Within the immigration system they have not only a right to sponsor but a right to appeal in a sponsorship program. Visitors do not have that right. I hope Members opposite would concede that there is a difference between visitors and permanent residents.
The purpose of the process outlined in Section 2 of this Bill is to make sure that there is maximum fairness provided to those who have been investigated and who have been issued a certificate. Therefore, in order to provide maximum fairness it seems to us that you can get that by appealing to the Federal Court. The Hon. Member for Spadina said that the court was not competent to hear this evidence. I hope he will rethink the suggestion that the court system is not competent to hear evidence. What is it all about if it is not competent to hear evidence, Mr. Speaker? Surely that is the very business in which the court is engaged. If the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) together with the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) make application on the basis of security information to a Federal Court, the very competentcy of the Federal Court guarantees that the person named in that application will get maximum fairness because that decision will be made in fact and in law. Therefore, I am somewhat perplexed at the persistence on the part of the Member from Spadina in raising this matter constantly.
The Member from Spadina says there will be Charter challenges. There is no escaping that because lawyers litigate. That is what they are all about. I think it is clear that there is good argument to be made that the Charter deals with people who are similarly situated. Surely the Member will agree, and
August 31, 1987

we are confident that the court will agree that visitors and permanent residents are not similarly situated.
Finally, the Member mentions that there is a backlog in the court system. There is a backlog in the immigration appeal division but not in the trial division where expertise has been developed in determination of fact.
1 cannot accept what the Member from Spadina and the Hon. Member for Davenport have said regarding this amendment. We cannot support the amendment. 1 do not think the Member from Spadina has dealt with Clause 4. It would be interesting for him to deal with, but he has not chosen to do that and I am surprised he chose to deal with this clause. At any rate, for these reasons, we cannot support the amendment proposed by the Member from Spadina.

I would simply say that the whole system of segregating out visitors or others who are not permanent residents or citizens as established by Clause 4 is what I wish to reject. However, I wish to take this occasion to respond to a couple of points made by the Parliamentary Secretary.
The Parliamentary Secretary talked about the court being competent to judge questions of evidence. In fact, the court's main expertise is to judge questions of procedure. According to its jurisdiction, it spends less time by far judging questions of evidence per se. It may judge a question of unreasonable disregard of evidence. Cases like that are often sent back to the jurisdictions from which they came for rehearing.
I notice that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary did not really challenge the point that the Federal Court does not have any specific expertise in security matters. The Security Intelligence Review Committee has that specific expertise. Therefore, the point I was making has not really been addressed or negated by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary.
The Parliamentary Secretary has said that visitors are not situated similarly to permanent residents. That is true, but the Supreme Court heard that argument in the case of Singh, the judgment it gave two and a half years ago. At that time, the court said in effect that when it is a matter of risk of life or imprisonment, the difference of situation between a permanent and a non-permanent resident is not enough to deny the normal due process to the non-permanent resident. It is true, as the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said, that when it comes to a question of the right to take employment in Canada, there is a difference. That difference is legislated and, to the best of my knowledge, it has not been challenged at the Supreme Court, though I am not familiar with all the cases.
It was interesting that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary made a sort of facetious reference to the possibility of Charter challenges. He said that of course lawyers will litigate, implying that lawyers will litigate frivolously or that they may have some rich clients who will hire them to litigate frivolously. It reminds me of the remark made by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) a couple of months ago when confronted with the fact that lawyers in private practice with expertise in immigration matters who had spoken publicly on the Bill had all spoken against Bill C-55. The Minister responded by saying: "Oh, they are just interested in their fees".
I find it remarkable that a lawyer who is simply interested in fees would be taking up the case of refugees who are mostly very poor. Except for the occasional one who may have made a fortune dealing in drugs in Vietnam and has retired as a general in Canada, refugees are not usually regarded as rich clients.
I also find it very interesting that this has come from a Government which has been preaching for nearly three years that it is the private sector that is the engine of recovery. 1 find
it very comical that this Government, which is selling off public corporations as fast as it can, this Government which has boasted that it will reduce the number of people in public employment, should speak with scorn about or try to denigrate lawyers in private practice.
I do not know if the Minister really thinks that all those lawyers ought to be hired by the Government, and I do not know if the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary thinks that they all ought to be civil servants before their opinions should be taken into consideration. 1 understand, of course, that lawyers hired by the Government have some difficulty expressing opinions in disagreement with the Government unless they have plans for other employment.
I find it strange that the Government should offer public scorn to the opinion of lawyers in the private sector whose only apparent offence from the Government's point of view is that they might want fees for their work.
I hope the Government will reconsider and will have some regard for lawyers in private practice, especially since it was lawyers in private practice who obtained the Singh decision against the expertise of government lawyers. 1 think it would be foolish on the part of the Government to dismiss the possibility of litigation brought by lawyers in private practice as though it were badly motivated and ineffective. I would ask Parliament to uphold this motion to delete Clause 3.

Mr. Speaker, we argue in favour of deleting Clause 3 for the reasons to which we already referred earlier. It would be difficult to add new information to the argument.
I would only like to bring to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary and the Government once again the comments on Clauses 2 and 3 of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. The High Commissioner made the important point that the first and most important thing is to determine whether or not a person is a refugee. That is the paramount decision that must be made. That must be done first because that is the nature of the matter affecting the future of a person who applies as a refugee, relying on us as a nation complying with our international agreements. The decision on security must then be made, but as a subsequent step.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees has registered an important message with the Government of Canada and that message has been ignored. That is why we feel that Clause 3 ought to be deleted.
All of a sudden, the experience of the committee is being put aside and a new process is being put into place that deals more with procedure than evidence, as the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) so eloquently put it. We feel that that is not the wise approach.
Reference has also been made to the possibility of this clause being found unconstitutional, and not simply for the fun of hiring lawyers and taking the Government of Canada to

court. There may be some very good grounds for taking the Government to court on this legislation in light of our Constitution.
For the life of me, I cannot understand why the Government takes this matter so lightly and ignores the submissions, comments and suggested amendments made by the committee. That is not good Government and it is not the open and democratic approach this Government promised in 1984. As a matter of fact, one can hardly find one comment or one suggested amendment made by the groups and individuals who appeared before the committee that has been accepted. In this case, this is an attitude of neglect on the part of the Government which is extremely difficult for us in Opposition to understand.

He drew a fairly long bow with respect to my remark regarding litigation. As usual for the NDP, sooner or later it comes down to money. Motion No. 9
That Bill C-84 be amended by deleting Clause 4.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the clause the Parliamentary Secretary was waiting for. 1 hope I have now satisfied his yearning because 1 am going to speak on it as he so much wanted me to do. I see him looking very happy and his disappointment is assuaged.
This clause is basically unnecessary and therefore unfair. It is not a question of whether Canada has the right and should have the power to protect itself against persons who may threaten our security or who otherwise are serious offenders in our eyes, people such as war criminals. That is not the question. We have dealt with war criminals in Bill C-71. We have provided for their inclusion under the Immigration Act. My Party supported both those decisions. What is at stake here is the refugee determination system for those people. That is why I and my Party oppose Clause 4 and have asked for its deletion.
I am advised that the Security Review Committee meets monthly, is flexible and can meet more often, as it has had occasion to do. It can meet in panels, even panels of one. It is very flexible in its approach. It has not caused any delay in the hearing of security cases which have come before it. Any delay was not caused by the inability of the committee to meet expeditiously. It was caused by the inability of CSIS to provide the information on which the committee could meet. If CSIS does not provide the data, then neither the committee nor the Federal Court can handle the case. Therefore, there is no ground for predicting that these cases could not be handled expeditiously.
In fact, the committee was told that the two functions of the security committee actually assist each other. That is to say, the examination of the particular cases, as under the Immigration Act, together with other cases, actually assists in elucidating the possible problems the Security Review Committee has

August 31, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
to examine in the operation of CSIS. That was explained to us by the chairman of the committee.
It is very important that this committee not operate in a vacuum, only examining abstract reports. It is very important that it have access to particular cases so it can see not only the analysis but the facts on which the analysis is based. For example, there were several cases of people who came from Chile. They were admitted as permanent residents but are now being accused of being security risks. That was the information provided by CSIS. But CSIS had not evaluated that information adequately. Perhaps that is not its function. At any rate, it did not. It simply said we have this information which is very damaging to those persons with respect to security.
The matter was brought to the security review committee and, operating with their knowledge of the security operations of Canada, and in dealing with counsel for the Chileans concerned, it turned out that all the evidence against those persons was based on information from the Pinochet Government which those persons had fled. It was either police reports originating from the Pinochet police or newspaper reports originating from newspapers owned or controlled by the Pinochet Government.
It is commonplace that a dictatorial Government, and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will not dispute the dictatorial nature of the Pinochet Government, tries to persecute people who have left the country after opposing the Government and trying to organize a democratic resistance. When they are finally chased out of the country in fear of their lives or liberty, a Government such as Pinochet's will pursue them with lies. It will try to compromise them in the eyes of whatever country they may go to. That is what happened in the case of these Chileans.
Therefore, it was very important for those persons that the Security Intelligence Review Committee reviewed their cases. It was also very important for the work of the SIRC in monitoring, overseeing and evaluating the work of our security service. It would not be to the benefit of Canada to separate the business of looking at particular cases such as this from the over-all review and analysis by the SIRC. It would not be to the benefit of certain individuals concerned, in certain cases at least, and it would not be to the benefit of the over-all work of the review committee.
We are asking that the review committee continue to have the responsibility. If the Minister is concerned about delay, as the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary suggests, it would have been and may still be quite easy to put certain time requirements into the clause.
In fact, I moved such an amendment in committee but the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary and his colleagues in the government caucus, who say they are interested in speed, were not interested in speed at that time. They were not interested
in amendments to the clause which would require the SIRC to render its decisions within certain statutorily specified times.
Therefore, there is not much weight to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary's argument that they are concerned about SIRC being too slow. There is no evidence that SIRC would be too slow and there is no evidence that the Government is seriously concerned about speed.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the House will adopt my motion to delete Clause 4 which would resolve any doubt in the Minister's mind about whether I was giving undue attention to Clauses 2 and 3.

Mr. Speaker, we feel the same way. Much has been said on this matter in committee by my colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). He argued about the potential unconstitutionality of this process and about the necessity of deleting this clause.
It is interesting to note that if we do not delete this clause and the preceding one the Minister will be given enormous discretionary powers of his or her own. The decision of the Minister on the basis of a certificate will go forward to the Federal Court. The Federal Court will have to take upon itself the onus of deciding whether the reasons which led to the issuance of that certificate are valid, sound and proper. It seems to me that that is quite a lot for a court to have to decide on the basis of a political decision.
We believe that the alternative is a much better way of handling refugee cases than the one being proposed here. The method proposed here has too much of a political undertone and gives extensive powers to one person, namely, the Minister of Immigration of the day. It then shifts the entire responsibility of deciding whether the political decision is valid and ought to be accepted, namely whether the certificate is appropriate or not and whether the grounds upon which the decision was made are correct or not, to the court which must then examine a political decision. Therefore, we are very unhappy about this development and that is why we urge the deletion of this clause.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will respond first to the last comments made by the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) that this has political overtones. It is just the opposite. If it is turned over to the Federal Court it removes any kind of political overtones from the proceedings. The Member might argue that in some of the Immigration Appeal Boards in some of the regions there may have been some intrusion of politics. He may want to argue that, but I hope he would not argue that if an application is brought before the Federal Court it becomes political. After all, it is removing the politicians from the scene. The Minister together with the Solicitor General file an application on the basis of evidence presented by CSIS which puts it in a nonpolitical arena in the federal court system. I hope my friend from Davenport will understand that.
August 31, 1987

He also said that the Minister has enormous discretionary powers. It is just the opposite. It must be dealt with in fact and in law. He does not have discretionary powers. Once he files to the federal court system it is out of his hands and the court decides.
I would now like to respond to the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) who began by saying that that which is at stake is the refugee determination system. I could not agree more. That is exactly what is at stake in this section and that is why I cannot accept his proposal.
The system has been defrauded by misuse. He and 1 have heard of the case which was reported in the press not too long ago of someone from New York who was involved in a $50 million insurance fraud and came to Canada and applied for refugee status here. That is what makes the refugee determination system fall apart.
I will remind Members of the classes of people with which we are dealing. In Subsection 19(l)(d), (e), (f) and (g) and in 27(2)(c) there is reference to organized criminal activity, espionage or subversion against democratic government, subversion by force of any government and acts of violence or subversion by force of any government. It is people involved in that kind of thing with whom we are dealing.
The guarantee that there will be some fairness in this system is that the evidence which it is not in the public interest to have publicized will be heard in camera and the individual will be protected from having information about him disseminated through the media. This addresses the whole element of fairness.
My friend from Spadina talks about the Pinochet Government. 1 think all of us in the House recognize that he is no boy scout leader. It is not always pleasant living in Chile. The Member referred to the evidence which was accepted by CSIS and then thrown out by the review board. I hope he will be confident that the court will be competent enough to make the same kind of decision as the review committee could make. Surely if the review committee were brilliant enough to discard trumped up evidence on the basis of newspaper reports from Chile or statements made by the Pinochet Government, court justices will be able to see through that kind of scam too and will be competent to deal with it.
Therefore, I suggest that Clause 4 is at the heart of the entire system with which we are dealing and to accept the amendment by the Hon. Member for Spadina would be to gut the legislation. We could not accept that.

Mr. Speaker, I did not have the privilege of taking part in the committee when it considered this particular clause, but I want to echo the concerns that other people have raised about the kinds of "star chamber'' aspects of this legislation.
The argument made by the Government is that there may be security grounds related to people seeking to be refugees and therefore this is required. If I understand correctly, 1 do not believe that there have been security offences committed within Canada by any person who has been admitted to this country as a refugee.

Mr. Speaker, that is also the case with some people who try to obtain refugee status and against whom allegations are made by the government of the country from which they came. As my hon. friend from Spadina (Mr. Heap) said earlier, if, for instance, the testimony is given by the secret police of a country like Chile, a very repressive dictatorship, containing statements that the alleged refugee has committed offences against the security of their country, we do not know exactly how such testimony will be dealt with by a judge of the Federal Court of Canada. We can assume there will be some problems since one of the critics of the Bill has pointed out, with regard to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, that they have, on occasion, too readily accepted information on security from authorities in countries that are not democratic and in fact are dictatorships.
Mr. Speaker, the Government is proposing that, if a person is suspected of being a possible threat to Canada's security- and as I just said in English, we have very little, in fact no proof that this has been a problem in the past-that in this case, instead of referring the evidene to an adjudicator who knows the immigration sector, instead of having that, we start over with a new process. The Federal Court of Canada is a very busy court. Even if, according to the Bill, a judge of the Federal Court must examine the certificate within seven days, there is no guarantee that the person in question has the right to know what the charges are against him. In some cases, that person will have no idea what the allegations are, since the judge will have the right, at the Government's request, to deny all access to information referred to the Court, on the basis of which the Government wants to prevent that person from being admitted to Canada.

I simply question the necessity for this entire heavy-handed kind of clause which again does not relate to evidence that we have had in Canada that people coming here as refugees have proven to be risks to Canadian security. They may be dealt with as security risks in Guatemala or Chile, which is precisely why they may be coming here. They are considered by those Governments to be a threat to the security of those states and are therefore being persecuted. They would not be a threat under our terms, but in seeking such simple things as dignity, land reform for peasants and better income, they are deemed to be in opposition to a government that may not be democratic.
That is why I support the efforts of my colleague, the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), and other Members, and say that if a process related to security questions is needed, it does not need to be heavy-handed in this way.
If it is needed, it does not need to be shunted into a different channel. There is no reason why it cannot be handled through the regular process of determination of refugees.
Of course, if there are security questions which trouble the Canadian authorities, then there needs to be a fast-track. However, the problem with the refugee determination process over-all is that there has not been adequate swift disposition of cases. If there was swift disposition of cases this type of instrument would not be needed and fast-tracking would probably not be required as well.

It makes its determinations on the basis of evidence, not on the basis of suspicion. It is staffed by justices who have been trained in law
and weighing evidence. It is our judgment that the claimant will have the best hearing if he is heard by a court of law.

Mr. Speaker, it is not as easy as the Parliamentary Secretary would have the House of Commons believe. In the last number of weeks we have heard representatives from a wide range of organizations, including the Civil Liberties Association of Canada. They mention that with this particular aspect of security plus a detainment certificate, potential claimants for refugee status are being treated, on suspicion, worse than the criminal who would rob a bank in broad daylight. Second, the United Nations High Commission for Refugees has expressed a great deal of concern about this particular clause.

subsubtopic: DEEP SEA DRIFT-NETS-KILLING OF MAMMALS AND SEABIRDS
speechtext:
As you know, Mr. Speaker, deep sea drift-nets are the marine equivalent of strip mining. Individually they hang to a depth of seven metres and often stretch for 50 kilometres.
In the Pacific Ocean alone there are an estimated 30,000 kilometres of drift-nets laid by 1,700 ships which belong to South Korea, Japan and Taiwan. The nets are intended to catch salmon and squid but also trap and kill up to 50,000 mammals such as whales, dolphins and sea lions, and one million seabirds.
Strung together these nets would reach from Tokyo, across Canada, to Rome. This shocking and wasteful method of fishing must be stopped before mammal, seabird and fish populations are depleted. The International Whaling Commission could stop this unacceptable exploitation of our common resources. We urge the Government of Canada to condemn Japan, South Korea and Taiwan strongly for using drift-net fishing, and to lead an international campaign to stop this practice.
August 31, 1987

S. 0. 21 SPORTS SPORTS IMMIGRANT SPRINTER BEN JOHNSON WINS WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP GOLD MEDAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many people have criticized the Government for its policy of steadily decreasing the number of immigrants admitted to this country. Some have asked just what have they added to Canada? The example of Ben Johnson is not a single example. He is the most celebrated of us all today, a world-class name, but he is only one of hundreds of thousands, in fact of millions of people who have come from various countries and have made Canada a better country.

subtopic: CALL FOR CONTINUATION OF BOOK RATE
CALL FOR CONTINUATION OF BOOK RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to bring to the attention of the House what is probably a very little known fact. It is that the Government subsidizes the transfer of books from libraries to citizens and between libraries. This is called the book rate.
This rate has been under active review ever since the Nielsen Task Force Report. Libraries have been unable to get any assurance that the subsidy will continue, and therefore that this service will continue.
How much are we talking about in dollars and cents? The Library association assures me that we are talking about potential increases of 400 per cent to 900 per cent. As one example, in Halifax County the increase there could be as high as 1,100 per cent. These are massive increases in costs for libraries.
The people who will be affected are those who are unable to have access to libraries, people in small rural communities. This is another attack on rural Canadian life. The blind and disabled will be affected, people who do not have easy access to library services. The elderly, who cannot find their way to libraries, will be affected. Students who are taking courses outside the city where their university may be located will also suffer.
This is a service that must continue. It is time for the Government to wake up and remember that the Post Office is a public service. It is not a private profit-making business. This is not an opportunity for the Conservative Government to continue to attack ordinary Canadians and their services.

OPENING OF BETHANY CARE CENTRE IN AIRDRIE, ALTA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday it was my pleasure to represent the Hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) at the official opening of the Bethany Care Centre in the City of Airdrie.
The complex consists of a 24-bed wing for brain-injured patients, a 50-bed seniors lodge, and a 50-bed nursing home. Each corridor has a street name and each room a house number, with individual thermostats, a window, and its own colour, while sinks, mirrors, et cetera are constructed to accommodate the aged and the disabled. There is a chapel, a crafts room, a greenhouse, a training centre and an auditorium-in fact everything to provide the best possible physical, social, spiritual and emotional care.
I commend the Lutheran Welfare Society of Alberta and all its members for sponsoring this splendid complex that will continue the long tradition of the Lutheran Society in providing care in a loving Christian manner. In fact, the Christian care for others permeates the entire complex. 1 commend the Government of Canada and the Government of Alberta for sharing in this project that will keep costs down to an affordable level.
This participation shows that the federal Government and the Government of Alberta really care for our aged, our injured and our disabled.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to either the Deputy Prime Minister or the Minister for International Trade. It is with regard to the preliminary tariff imposed by the U.S. Trade Commission of up to 85.2 per cent on Canadian potash imported into that country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade
subtopic: UNITED STATES TARIFF ON CANADIAN POTASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I categorically deny that there has been any government indecision on this trade action brought by the U.S. We have worked with the industry from the start of this dispute to review the system. It is a dispute between the U.S. industry and Canadian producers. We have offered every possible assistance. I already stated when this decision came down that our view has been that this action should never have been brought because the companies that brought the action against the Canadian producers account for less than 5 per cent of the U.S. production.
As the Hon. Member probably understands, the United States only produces about 10 per cent of its own potash requirements. To bring an action against their major supplier does not make economic sense. As the Member already pointed out, the people who will pay for this in the long run are the U.S. farm producers and U.S. consumers.

Mr. Speaker, before lunch 1 was debating Motion No. 9 moved by my colleague from the New Democratic Party. This is an amendment that is very similar to my Motion No. 10. It concerns provisions for the security certificate that we would like to amend.
What we are suggesting is that if in fact the individual claimant is found to be some kind of a security threat or falls within an undesirable category within the Immigration Act, then by all means we are supportive of detaining that individual to ascertain his identification to see whether or not there is sufficient cause to merit that individual's further detention or deportation.
Our concerns articulated by my Motion No. 10, and by Motion No. 9 which we are presently debating, are that under the current legislation any individual who is deemed to have been the recipient of such a security certificate would not necessarily have the opportunity of entering into the refugee determination process. The provision as stated in Bill C-84
would restrict accessibility to the system and undermine the crucial universality component.
Many times a certificate may be granted based on information received from the country of origin. In the case of real refugees, often it is not unusual for the government of the country from which they are escaping to provide Canada, or another country receiving that claimant, with information that would suggest that that person is either an undesirable or poses a security threat. For instance, an individual in another country may be seen as an offender, for standing up for democracy. Obviously within our system of justice, and within the Canadian parameters, someone who stands up for democracy, as we do every single day, would not be considered a security threat or an undesirable. Many times information received from the country or the government of origin would actually substantiate the fact that the person's case is probably legitimate, that is, because of political or religious pressures that individual is escaping as a refugee under the definition of the United Nations Convention.
Our first concern is that by declaring this certificate, it would override or ignore the very information that can be utilized to determine and substantiate the individual's true refugee claim. However, if Canadian authorities find the claim to merit further consideration, then that individual should not be sent back to the country from which he or she is escaping because he or she may be in some particular trouble, may face certain persecution, torture, imprisonment, or probable death.
Another aspect that colours this particular clause is that if we deny accessibility to individuals to have their case properly determined within the refuge board or the refugee system where the issue is properly disposed of rather than making a predetermined determination by the Minister or his official, that is of great concern to our United Nations obligations under the Geneva Convention. In fact, a representative of the United Nations High Commission appeared before the legislative committee which was studying Bill C-84 and expressed considerable reservation concerning this particular clause which would guarantee that an individual would not be allowed to pursue the refugee process and would be deported and expelled from the country.
That runs contrary to the non-refoulement undertaking that we as a country have given under the United Nations Convention. Therefore, it was not without passing concern from the United Nations High Commission that these representations were made at the committee, and in correspondence exchanged between the High Commissioner for Refugees and the Government of Canada. I believe there has been considerable concern expressed internationally that, if Canada enacts this particular legislation with this particular clause as it stands, it would be undermining the non-refoulement undertaking.
Since Canada has been at the leadership level in terms of providing and offering leadership for the salvaging of the plight facing refugees, the concern is that other countries may legislate similar clauses. If that happened on a frequent basis
August 31, 1987

one can see the danger of the United Nations Geneva Convention coming apart, and the very foundation being rocked. In the correspondence from the High Commissioner for Refugees to the Government of Canada there was a specific paragraph that suggested and reminded Canada that this could trigger an exodus by other countries.
It is with that spirit that we spoke to it in committee, and witnesses participated, to ensure that if the person is a security threat, or if there is need for detainment, then by all means a certificate or the powers should be available. However, this should not exclude the individual from receiving a hearing in order to properly determine if the concerns are founded and, if they are founded, what repercussions that person would face if he or she was returned to the country from which he or she was fleeing.
Our amendments suggest that the current legislation which allows an individual to participate in the refugee determination system be retained and, therefore, protect our international obligations and our obligations under the accessibility and universality of the system.

Motion No. 8
Immigration Act, 1976
That Bill C-84 be amended in Clause 4 by striking out lines 29 to 31 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"officer or an adjudicator shall make an order to detain or release the person named in the"
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a relatively simple point in Clause 4. Clause 4 represents an amending of the Act in connection with detention of a person:
-where the Minister and the Solicitor General are of the opinion, based on security or criminal intelligence reports received and considered by them, that a person, other than a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, is a person described in paragraphs 19(l)(d), (e), (f) or (g), or 27(2)(c), they may sign and file a certificate to that effect with an immigration officer, a senior immigration officer or an adjudicator.
This is not the security certificate previously referred to in an earlier section. Perhaps this could be called a detention certificate. In proposed Subsection 41(2), which is the one I am dealing with, it states:
(2) Where a certificate is signed and filed in accordance with subsection (1), an inquiry under this Act concerning the person in respect of whom the certificate is filed shall not be commenced, or if commenced shall be adjourned, until the determination referred to in paragraph (4)(d) has been made and a senior immigration officer or an adjudicator shall, notwithstanding section 23 or 104, detain or make an order to detain the person named in the certificate until the making of the determination.
This concerns the making of a certificate which suggests that a certain person who is seeking entry is perhaps a criminal or a threat to the security of Canada.
What the second paragraph does, which I seek to amend, is to make it compulsory that that person be detained. An adjudicator has the power to make a decision. He is a quasi judge. An adjudicator normally is allowed to make the decision to detain or not to detain. The wording in this clause is that a senior immigration officer or an adjudicator shall notwithstanding detain, which means removing the power of the adjudicator to do what essentially an adjudicator does. I do not think it has been shown that that is necessary, Mr. Speaker. What we have been told is that people may require a longer time to investigate, but we have not been shown that inexperienced adjudicators have failed to detain people on their own judgment when given an indication by the Minister that that is something which they ought to do.
I think it is an unfortunate tendency to take away from a lower official, that is, lower than the Minister, the power he has been exercising according to law and that as far as I know he has exercised satisfactorily for the Government. I have not heard complaints that adjudicators have been irresponsibly turning people loose whom the Minister wanted detained longer. However, I have heard complaints that adjudicators have not turned people loose when some people thought they should. I even heard of one situation where it was reliably reported that the Minister thought the adjudicator should turn some people loose but still did not. It seems to me that if the adjudicator has erred, the adjudicator has erred on the side of caution, that is, detaining a person to make sure that the matter was cleared up so far as necessary.

August 31, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
I believe that in this case it is unreasonable to assume that the adjudicator would act irresponsibly when presented with a Minister's certificate. Granted, the adjudicator does not have all the information behind the certificate, but I believe that adjudicators have shown themselves responsible in this matter of security.
Therefore, I proposed the motion to delete lines 29, 30 and 31 replacing them so that the clause would read:
-a senior immigration officer or an adjudicator shall make an order to
detain or release the person named in the certificate-
1 believe that would respect the existing law in that it would allow the adjudicator to perform his or her function, he, being the man or woman on the spot who is in possession of the essential facts, including the Minister's certificate. It would allow that person to do the job that he or she should do without being overruled and turned into a mere rubber stamp by the Act, as is the case the way the Act is now worded.
I would ask Members of the House to vote for this motion to sustain, to keep intact, the responsibility of the adjudicator in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address Motion No. 8. The motion is very similar to one I presented at the legislative committee which was, as all amendments were, turned down.
The reason I presented the motion then and the reason 1 speak in favour of it now is that we heard very moving testimony about the need for a check and balance. The arguments received at committee and the arguments that I put forward were not for detainment of individuals in respect of whom government officials had no identification, or that particularly valuable information was received on a claimant. That was not the concern. We are not saying that a person should not be detained. Existing legislation provides full opportunity for an individual to be detained for 48 hours without going to an adjudicator. Subsequent to that the Minister, the Crown or officials can go to an adjudicator and request detainment of an additional seven days. The question is, who makes the decision and how is it made.
A presentation by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association articulated very thoughtfully about the need to have the adjudicator make the decision based on evidence that he or she receives from the Government. In other words, the information provided to the adjudicator would be analysed and considered rather than giving total power, carte blanche if you will, to the Minister of the day. That would be seen as excessive power or unilateral power allowing the Minister to detain an individual without having to go to an adjudicator. That is why many witnesses, and certainly the leading one on this clause, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, argued for the need of a politically disinterested decision-maker rather than a politically motivated or politically interested individual. It was not meant to be a slight against the Minister or a Minister's position, but obviously it was referring to the realities of a Minister or to the realities of politicians.
You and I, Mr. Speaker, and everyone else in this Chamber receive various representations. We push and pull situations on a number of issues. Quite often from what we hear, feel and see we make a decision. The argument here is to offer protection in the system so that the Minister's powers would not be abused and misused. Again, it is not a slight against the current Minister. We are talking here about Ministers, certainly long after the present Minister and after you and I are gone, Mr. Speaker.
The request was for the adjudicator to have the flexibility and discretion of saying, "The information I receive from the Government justifies its concern and therefore, justifies further detainment". Or, perhaps based on information the adjudicator receives from the Government or other sources he will say, "Hold on, the preconceived notions are unfounded because I found a, b, c and d" which would then be offered to the Government. The Government would then have a further opportunity of rebutting the case or saying, "You are correct, Mr. Adjudicator". This offers a check and balance.
The current legislation offers those checks and balances. That point was accepted by Canadians at large that, yes, we have the powers to detain, but detain in a way to ensure that people's rights are protected and that powers are not abused and misused.
I believe the motion I put forward at committee and the very similar motion that we are debating here this afternoon is a very reasonable one, with which most Canadians would agree, given the sense of justice within this country.
I urge the House to adopt the motion so that we retain the discretion of the adjudicator, who would be in a position of being politically disinterested, borrowing a phrase from the Canadian Civil Liberties Association. If we move on this it would ensure that our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, for which we have fought so hard, will not be challenged and it will also preclude any court challenges in the future on this particular clause. A number of legal experts suggested that this would be one of the clauses that would bring a Charter challenge under Section 8. I do not, and I am sure that neither you, Mr. Speaker, nor any other Member of this House, would want this legislation to become policy of the Government, get tied up in the courts, paralyzing our policies. If that happens six months, 12 months or 18 months down the line, Canadians will not have patience or trust in the Government any more. They want the Government and Parliament to do it right this time.
We were called back for an emergency and I would not want to leave this Chamber without the provisions of the Bill being legally accepted. If they are not, the refugee system and particularly the Government will pay a bigger price once these challenges begin to take shape in the courts. Therefore, it is with that spirit in mind that I hope the Government will move to retain the discretion of the adjudicator and allow him or her
August 31, 1987

to make the decision based on information provided by the Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) began by saying that this is a simple point. In terms of an amendment it may be very simple, but its effect would be very complicating both in terms of the administration of the system and the security of Canadians.
I would reiterate what I said before lunch on the previous amendment. We are dealing with what is broadly called the inadmissible class of people, those who have records of criminality, organized criminal activity, espionage or subversion against democratic Governments, subversion by force of any Government, or acts of violence or subversion by force of any Government. Those are the kinds of people about whom we are talking.
The difference between the position of government Members and that of Members of the Opposition is on whether we should release or detain these individuals under certain circumstances. The Hon. Member for Spadina read certain clauses of the Bill as it is now before the House. Clause 41(1) indicates that the Minister may sign and file a certificate to that effect. He is not obligated to do so and may do so depending upon the circumstances of the case. It may be that he is presented with old information. However, if he chooses to sign and file a certificate, then Clause 41(2) comes into effect and provides the following:
Where a certificate is signed and filed in accordance with subsection (1), an
inquiry under this Act concerning the person in respect of whom the certificate
is filed shall not be commenced, or if commenced shall be adjourned,-
That is the simple point. If there has been evidence to convince the Minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) to file a certificate, then there are not many options left. The primary obligation is to protect the security of Canada and Canadians.
I would remind Hon. Members of what I said in committee the other day when I referred to the Bill of 1976. A distinction was made between whether coming to Canada is a privilege or a right. Most Canadians believe that it is a privilege to be in Canada. The amendments we are now debating make it look almost as though it were a right for inadmissible classes of people to maintain freedom of movement in Canada.
I would like to underscore the fact that the primary obligation of the Government, and in fact of all of us, is to protect the security of the country and of individual Canadians. The fact is that this amendment would make the detention of security risks difficult if not impossible. As well, the information on which the Ministers base their decision to file a certificate is not information that can be released to the adjudicator, so it is not surprising that in times past, adjudicators have released individuals who should not have been released and did so with all good intent. In the past, the Government has been unable to obtain an order for detention from an adjudicator in security cases because the adjudicator was not aware of the risks involved.
Immigration Act, 1976
Turning back to the Hon. Member's point, it is very simple. Do we detain or set at liberty those who the Minister and the Solicitor General are convinced are security risks? The Government must opt for the security of Canada and of individual Canadians.
